ch15.anchor: deputy general manager of the Zhejiang Industrial Bank
ch15.note: Zhang Naiqi was a prominent banker and essayist. He later became one of the “Seven Gentlemen” of the National Salvation Association, arrested by the Nationalists in 1936 for pressing for resistance to Japan, and after 1949 served as the People’s Republic’s first minister of food.

ch15.anchor: Beishanxi Road, in the International Settlement.
ch15.note: So printed in the source, here and again just below. There was no “Beishanxi Road” in the Shanghai settlements; the name is almost certainly a slip for Shanxi North Road, a street in the northern part of the International Settlement.—Trans.

ch15.anchor: when Kirov, a member of the Politburo of the Soviet Communist Party, was assassinated
ch15.note: Sergei Kirov, the Leningrad party chief and a member of the Soviet Politburo, was shot dead on December 1, 1934. Stalin used the killing as the pretext for the terror that became the Great Purge, in which the hunt for alleged “Trotskyists” swept up Soviet and foreign Communists alike, the Chinese students in Moscow among them.

Georgi Dimitrov (1882–1949), the Bulgarian Communist who had won worldwide fame by turning his own defense at the 1933 Reichstag-fire trial in Nazi Germany into an indictment of the Nazis, was elected general secretary of the Comintern at its Seventh Congress in 1935. He became the public face of its new line of a broad united front against fascism.

The “August First Declaration” marked the CCP’s public turn from the class-war line of the soviet years toward a national united front against Japan. Issued in the name of the Chinese Soviet government and the Party Center, it was in fact drafted by the CCP delegation in Moscow around the time of the Comintern’s Seventh Congress, and it prefigured the second Nationalist–Communist alliance of 1937.

ch15.anchor: brothers who quarrel within the walls still join to repel insult from without
ch15.note: An allusion to the Book of Songs (Shijing): “Brothers may quarrel within the walls, yet outside they defend one another against insult.” The classical line is invoked to urge Nationalists and Communists to set aside their civil war and unite against the Japanese.

The source names the Western agent only as “Walton,” a transliteration of the Chinese Hua’erdun; his identity is not established here. The 1935 prosecution belongs to the wave of trials of Comintern and Soviet military-intelligence networks in China that had begun with the arrest of the Noulens couple in 1931 (see Chapter Twelve).

Chen Yun’s account, written under the pen name “Lianchen” and cast as the notes of a captured doctor traveling with the Red Army, was the first substantial insider narrative of the Long March to reach the outside world; it appeared in the Communist Chinese press in Paris and Moscow in 1936.

“Zhu-Mao” joins the names of Zhu De, the Red Army’s commander-in-chief, and Mao Zedong, its political leader. From the late 1920s the two were so bound up with the force that outsiders sometimes took “Zhu Mao” for the name of a single man.

ch15.anchor: today it has become a prairie fire
ch15.note: An echo of Mao Zedong’s celebrated 1930 essay, whose title is usually given in English as “A Single Spark Can Start a Prairie Fire” (from the classical saying that a single spark can set the whole plain ablaze).
